speaker: Chris Olah
title: What the hell is going on inside neural networks? | Chris Olah
question: When building safe frontier AI models, why shouldn't you try to eliminate safety risks by simply removing internal representations of offensive or harmful concepts?
guest: Yeah, I think it's tricky to get rid of these things. I think it's also not clear that you actually want to get rid of the representation of these things. There's a neuron that is like an offensiveness neuron—it responds to really bad stuff like swear words, racial slurs, really offensive things. On the one hand, you might say, "We should get rid of that neuron; it's not good to have a neuron that responds to those things." On the other hand, part of the function of that neuron could actually be to pair images that are offensive with captions that rebut them, because people will post an image and then respond to it. And that's the thing you would actually like it to do: recognize offensive content and rebut it. My personal intuition is that we don't want models that don't understand these things; we want models that understand these things and respond appropriately to them. It's not like we would prevent children from ever finding out about racism and sexism—rather, we want to educate them that racism and sexism are bad and how to thoughtfully navigate those issues.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because a model needs to understand harmful concepts in order to behave safely around them. Recognizing and refusing a dangerous request, detecting deception or abuse, moderating content, helping defenders, and reasoning about ethics all depend on having a representation of what harm is. A model with no concept of, say, a bioweapon or manipulation can't notice when it is being steered toward one, so removing the concept removes the safeguard along with the risk.

It also doesn't work well in practice. Concepts in neural networks are not stored in neat, isolated places; they are distributed and entangled with benign, useful knowledge (chemistry, medicine, security, history). Ablating them tends to degrade general capability, and the knowledge is often only suppressed rather than erased: it can be recovered through fine-tuning, jailbreaks, or reconstructed from adjacent facts the model still has. Many harmful capabilities are also dual-use, so there is no clean line to cut along.

The more robust goal is a model that understands harmful concepts but reliably chooses not to act harmfully, where safety comes from its values and judgment, backed by external safeguards, rather than from ignorance.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Removing internal representations of harmful or offensive concepts actually undermines safety because a model cannot reliably avoid or refuse dangers it can no longer recognize. Safety mechanisms depend on those very representations to detect malicious intent, trigger refusals, moderate toxic content, and power internal monitoring probes; blinding a model to what constitutes harm leaves it easily manipulated into executing dangerous steps or generating offensive outputs it fails to perceive as risky. Moreover, neural representations are deeply entangled and dual-use: concepts underlying cyberattacks, pathogens, or abuse overlap heavily with legitimate knowledge essential for defensive cybersecurity, medicine, law, and history, so erasing them inflicts severe collateral damage on benign capabilities. Finally, concept removal creates a false sense of security. Because frontier models reason compositionally from first principles, they can reconstruct dangerous procedures from benign foundational facts or rapidly recover suppressed concepts through in-context prompting or minimal fine-tuning, while hiding those dynamics from interpretability tools. Robust safety therefore requires preserving a model’s comprehension of harm while aligning its behavior and monitoring its intact internal states.

noweb.answer: Removing internal representations of harmful or offensive concepts makes a model blinder rather than safer, primarily because recognizing harm is a prerequisite for preventing it. To reliably refuse dangerous requests, moderate toxic text, or detect subtle jailbreaks, a model must first understand what constitutes abuse, violence, or exploitation. Furthermore, most sensitive concepts are contextual and dual-use: the same underlying knowledge involved in cyberattacks, toxins, or hate speech is essential for defensive cybersecurity, medical care, historical education, and supporting victims. Erasing those concepts cripples legitimate, beneficial applications. Finally, concepts inside neural networks are distributed and entangled rather than neatly isolated. Attempting to surgically delete them degrades general reasoning while failing to eliminate risk, because a capable frontier model can still reconstruct dangerous outputs from benign building blocks and first principles. Effective alignment therefore relies not on enforced ignorance, but on models that understand harmful concepts clearly enough to exercise sound, context-aware judgment about how to respond.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Removing harmful concepts from a model's internal representations sounds like a clean fix, but it tends to backfire for a few reasons.

First, a model has to understand harm in order to handle it safely. Recognizing a dangerous request, refusing it well, flagging toxic content, explaining why something is risky, and helping defenders (security analysts, content moderators, clinicians) all depend on the model having a clear internal picture of those concepts. A model that can't represent a harm can't reliably see it coming. Research on pretraining data supports this: models that saw some toxic data built cleaner, more separable toxicity representations, which made them easier to detect and steer away from bad outputs.

Second, concepts in neural networks are spread out and overlap heavily with one another (superposition). Cutting out "offensive" knowledge damages nearby harmless abilities like chemistry, biology, history and security, and usually leaves traces that fine-tuning or clever prompting can bring back. Studies on "unlearning" keep finding the removal is shallow.

Third, it weakens oversight. Interpretability tools and activation monitors need those features to exist so they can watch for and steer harmful behavior. A better approach is to keep the understanding and shape the model's values and behavior around it.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: Trying to make a frontier AI model safe by erasing its internal representations of offensive or harmful concepts fails for three main reasons. First, safety depends on recognition: to reliably refuse dangerous requests, moderate content, or catch subtle and adversarial prompts, a model must understand what constitutes harm and distinguish malicious intent from benign context. If it cannot represent a harmful concept, it cannot reliably detect or avoid it. Second, internal representations in neural networks are deeply entangled and dual-use. Knowledge of toxins, cyber vulnerabilities, or hate speech overlaps heavily with legitimate domains like medicine, defensive security, history, and law; excising those features degrades general capabilities and breaks valuable benign uses. Finally, concept removal is brittle and incomplete. Capable models can still reconstruct harmful information from benign building blocks or first-principles reasoning, and suppressed representations often resurface under jailbreaks or fine-tuning. Effective safety therefore requires shaping how a model evaluates and acts on sensitive concepts, not trying to blind it to them.

noweb.answer: Trying to eliminate safety risks by erasing internal representations of harmful concepts is counterproductive for several fundamental reasons. First, a model must understand what is harmful in order to reliably detect, evaluate, and refuse dangerous requests—especially when users employ subtle framing, metaphors, or adversarial jailbreaks. Removing those representations blinds the model to the very risks it needs to guard against. Second, neural networks store knowledge in deeply entangled, overlapping features, and much hazardous information is dual-use. Concepts tied to biosecurity, cybersecurity, chemistry, or hate speech overlap heavily with medicine, defensive engineering, history, and content moderation, so excising them severely degrades benign capabilities. Finally, representation removal is brittle: frontier models can still compose harmful outputs from benign building blocks at inference time or rapidly relearn suppressed concepts during fine-tuning. Effective safety therefore relies on preserving accurate conceptual understanding while shaping how the model reasons and acts on it.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A model needs to understand harmful concepts to recognize dangerous requests, explain risks, and help people prevent or respond to harm. Removing that understanding could weaken safeguards and make the model less useful in legitimate contexts, such as helping someone recognize a scam.

Concepts are also often encoded across many parts of a model and overlap with ordinary knowledge. Deleting a feature associated with a harmful concept can damage unrelated abilities while leaving the model able to reconstruct the concept or produce the same harmful behavior through another route.

A better safety target is what the model does with its knowledge. Train and evaluate it to distinguish legitimate requests from harmful ones, limit assistance that would enable harm, and test whether those safeguards hold under unfamiliar or adversarial prompts.

A model needs to recognize harmful concepts to respond safely. Spotting a threat, explaining why a slur is offensive, or helping someone respond to abuse all require understanding the content. Erasing that understanding could make the model worse at recognizing danger while leaving it capable of causing harm in ways the intervention missed.

Concepts also tend to be encoded across many overlapping patterns of activity. Removing one pattern may impair unrelated abilities, while other patterns can still support the same harmful behavior. A better safety goal is to shape and test how the model uses its knowledge in context. It should recognize when a request would facilitate harm, decline that assistance, and still help someone trying to prevent or recover from harm.
